guide.title: Sant'Angelo, Rome: the Portico d'Ottavia, the Teatro di Marcello and the old Jewish quarter
guide.intro: Sant'Angelo is R. XI, the eleventh of Rome's rioni by toponymic code, and it measures about 480 metres by 360 metres, roughly a tenth of a square kilometre. Inside that you can stand in front of the Portico d'Ottavia, the Teatro di Marcello with a Renaissance palace built on top of it, the Fontana delle Tartarughe and the Great Synagogue of Rome, and walk between them in a handful of streets. The rione holds the old Jewish quarter, enclosed by papal bull in 1555 and demolished in 1885, and the two museums that carry its history. It also holds ten churches, a whole block of Mattei family palaces, and a national museum that has been shut since January 2023. Almost every edge of the rione runs down the middle of a street or a square shared with a neighbour.

sections.heading: What is in Sant'Angelo, and what is not
sections.body:
Sant'Angelo has six land borders and every one of them runs along a named street or square. Roma Capitale's page for the rione gives the boundary as largo Arenula, via Florida, via delle Botteghe Oscure, via dell'Aracoeli, via and piazza Margana, via dei Delfini, via dei Cavalletti, via della Tribuna di Campitelli, via del Teatro di Marcello, via del Foro Olitorio, lungotevere de' Cenci, via del Progresso, piazza delle Cinque Scole, via di Santa Maria del Pianto, via in Publicolis and via di Sant'Elena. it.wikipedia's article on the rione gives a list that agrees in most of its length and adds via di Monte Savello, via Montanara and via dei Falegnami. A street named as a boundary tells you where the line runs, not what stands on either side of it.

The Isola Tiberina, ponte Fabricio and ponte Cestio are in Ripa. Palazzo Cenci, the Cenci streets and Santa Maria del Pianto are in Regola. Largo di Torre Argentina with its four Republican temples is in Pigna, and the archaeological area under via delle Botteghe Oscure, directly across the street from the Crypta Balbi, is in Pigna too: the Sovrintendenza Capitolina's own page for it gives Rione Pigna. Piazza Margana, the Capitoline hill and the museums on it are in Campitelli.

The restaurants people mean when they say the Ghetto's restaurants do not all sit in one rione. Piperno, Sora Margherita, Al Pompiere, Beppe e i suoi formaggi and Sheva stand across the line in Regola. Giggetto, Nonna Betta, Ba'Ghetto, BellaCarne, La Taverna del Ghetto, Renato al Ghetto and the Boccione bakery are in Sant'Angelo.

One name is worth explaining before you look for it on a map. Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli stands on piazza di Campitelli, and both the church and the square are in Sant'Angelo. it.wikipedia records that the building belonged originally to rione Campitelli and was attributed to Sant'Angelo when Sant'Angelo's boundaries were extended around the middle of the twentieth century.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source states a metro station or a bus route for the rione, so none is given here, and neither are walking times or distances. Steer by addresses.

The Museo Ebraico di Roma gives its address as via Catalana, in the Tempio Maggiore complex. The Fondazione Museo della Shoah ETS gives the Casina dei Vallati at via del Portico d'Ottavia 29. Roma Capitale gives the Museo Nazionale Romano Crypta Balbi at via delle Botteghe Oscure 31. The parish of Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli is at piazza di Campitelli 9. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives its own seat as piazza Lovatelli 35, and lists the Centro di Documentazione dell'Appia at via del Teatro di Marcello 5. Sala Santa Rita is at via Montanara 8, and Trattoria Giggetto at via del Portico d'Ottavia 21/A.

Several of those streets are rione boundaries: via delle Botteghe Oscure, via del Teatro di Marcello, via Montanara and piazza delle Cinque Scole all have another rione on the far side. An address on one of them is an address and nothing more. The streets that lie inside Sant'Angelo, and that this guide uses to orient rather than as records, are via del Portico d'Ottavia, via della Reginella, via Catalana, via del Tempio, via di Sant'Ambrogio, via di Sant'Angelo in Pescheria and via del Foro Piscario.

sections.heading: Tickets and opening hours
sections.body:
The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the Teatro di Marcello as open every day, 9.00 to 19.00 under summer time and 9.00 to 18.00 under winter time, entry free, closed on 1 May, and states that it is seen from the outside only. Roma Capitale gives the Portico d'Ottavia as always visitable, reached by a ramp and a cordonata.

The Museo Ebraico di Roma publishes its 2026 hours in bands. In winter: 1 to 26 October, Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 17.00, last admission 16.15, and Friday 9.00 to 14.00, last admission 13.15; 27 October to 9 November and 12 January to 8 February, Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 16.30, last admission 15.45, and Friday 9.00 to 14.00; 10 November to 11 January, Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 16.00, last admission 15.15, and Friday 9.00 to 14.00; 9 February to 31 March, Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 17.00 and Friday 9.00 to 14.00. In summer, 1 April to 30 September, Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 18.00, last admission 17.15, and Friday 10.00 to 16.00, last admission 15.15. It is closed on Saturdays and on Jewish holidays, and the museum publishes a dated closure calendar. Admission is 12.00 euro full, 6.00 euro for students up to 25 with proof and 10.00 euro on the agreement rate, free for children under 10, for visitors with certified disability above 74 per cent and a companion where needed, for ICOM and ICOMOS card holders, for police and armed forces and for accredited journalists; online transactions carry a 1.00 euro service commission. The ticket includes a guided visit to the Tempio Maggiore. Guided tours of the museum with the Tempio Maggiore and the Tempio Spagnolo are 100.00 euro for families and adult groups up to 25, plus admission; walking tours of the Jewish quarter are 100.00 euro for one to four people, 150.00 euro for five to fifteen and 10.00 euro a head for sixteen to thirty-five. Booking is online and at least five days ahead.

The Fondazione Museo della Shoah ETS gives the Casina dei Vallati as open Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 18.00 and Friday 10.00 to 13.00, excluding Jewish holidays, closed Saturday.

Roma Capitale states that from 9 January 2023 the Crypta Balbi has been closed to the public for the works connected with the URBS project. No reopening date is stated.

For the churches, the parish of Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli gives Mass at 10.00 and 18.30 on feast days and 7.30 and 18.30 on weekdays. No source states opening hours for Sant'Angelo in Pescheria, San Nicola in Carcere or Santa Caterina dei Funari, so none are given here. Roma Capitale gives Sala Santa Rita as open when an exhibition is running. Among the restaurants, Roma Capitale gives Trattoria Giggetto as Tuesday to Sunday 12.30 to 15.00 and 19.30 to 23.00, closed Monday, and Nonna Betta's own site gives 12.15 to 15.00 and 18.30 to 22.00, closed Tuesday.

faq.question: Is all of the Roman Ghetto in Sant'Angelo?
faq.answer: No. Roma Capitale describes the old Jewish quarter as situated inside Rione XI - Sant'Angelo, and the Portico d'Ottavia, the Tempio Maggiore, the Museo Ebraico, the Museo della Shoah at the Casina dei Vallati and via della Reginella are all here. But the rione boundary with Regola runs along piazza delle Cinque Scole, via di Santa Maria del Pianto and via del Progresso, and several of the restaurants a visitor would name as the Ghetto's stand on the far side of it: Piperno, Sora Margherita, Al Pompiere, Beppe e i suoi formaggi and Sheva are in Regola, as are Palazzo Cenci and the Cenci streets.

faq.question: Can you go inside the Great Synagogue?
faq.answer: Yes, through the Museo Ebraico di Roma. The museum states that its ticket includes a guided visit to the Tempio Maggiore, and it also runs longer guided tours that take in the Tempio Spagnolo, the Spanish-rite oratory placed in the same building in 1932. Admission is 12.00 euro full and 6.00 euro for students up to 25 with proof. The museum is closed on Saturdays and on Jewish holidays and publishes a dated closure calendar; on Fridays it shuts early, at 14.00 for most of the year and 16.00 between 1 April and 30 September.

faq.question: Is the Crypta Balbi open?
faq.answer: No. Roma Capitale states that from 9 January 2023 the Crypta Balbi has been closed to the public for the works connected with the URBS project, and no reopening date is stated. It is one of the four seats of the Museo Nazionale Romano, with Palazzo Massimo, Palazzo Altemps and the Terme di Diocleziano, and it stands at via delle Botteghe Oscure 31, over the porticoed courtyard behind the theatre Lucius Cornelius Balbus dedicated in 13 BC.

faq.question: Why is Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli not in Campitelli?
faq.answer: Because the boundary moved. it.wikipedia records that the church belonged originally to rione Campitelli and was attributed to rione Sant'Angelo when Sant'Angelo's boundaries were extended around the middle of the twentieth century, after the clearances of the Fascist period. The name it carries is older than the line. The square it stands on, piazza di Campitelli, is in Sant'Angelo too, together with the Palazzetto di Flaminio Ponzio at no. 6 and Palazzo Clementi.

faq.question: What is largo 16 Ottobre 1943?
faq.answer: A square in the Jewish quarter named for the round-up carried out there. Between 5.30 in the morning and two in the afternoon on 16 October 1943, SS and German order police, working from a census taken years earlier by the Fascist government, arrested 1,259 people in the square and the surrounding streets. Weeks earlier the community had been made to hand over fifty kilograms of gold against a promise of safety, and had done so. After foreign nationals and members of mixed families were released, 1,023 people were deported to Auschwitz; sixteen came back. The plaque in the square records 2,091 Roman Jews deported over the whole of the German occupation, of whom 101 returned.

faq.question: What can you actually get into in Sant'Angelo?
faq.answer: Two ticketed institutions with published hours: the Museo Ebraico di Roma, whose ticket includes the Tempio Maggiore, and the Fondazione Museo della Shoah at the Casina dei Vallati. The Teatro di Marcello is free and open daily, seen from the outside only, and the Portico d'Ottavia is given by Roma Capitale as always visitable. Sala Santa Rita, the deconsecrated church that Roma Capitale runs as an exhibition space, opens when an exhibition is on. The Crypta Balbi is closed. The churches keep their own arrangements; the parish of Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli publishes Mass times, which are not visiting hours.

photos.title: The Portico d'Ottavia
photos.description: The surviving propylaeum of the Portico d'Ottavia on via del Portico d'Ottavia, with the medieval brick arch that replaced two of its columns and the church of Sant'Angelo in Pescheria built into it behind.
photos.author: Jorge Franganillo

places.name: Portico d'Ottavia
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 29, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The surviving corner and propylaeum of a Roman quadriportico, and the object the whole quarter is organised around. The church of Sant'Angelo in Pescheria is built into the propylaeum. Roma Capitale gives it as always visitable, reached by a ramp and a cordonata.
places.history: Augustus rebuilt the portico between 27 and 23 BC in place of the earlier portico of Metellus, and dedicated it in the name of his sister Octavia. After a fire in 191 it was restored and largely rebuilt in 203 by Septimius Severus and Caracalla, and most of what stands is that rebuilding; the dedicatory inscription of 203 is still on the architrave, and the Sovrintendenza Capitolina carries its Latin text with an Italian translation. The quadriportico measured 119 by 132 metres and enclosed the temples of Juno Regina and Jupiter Stator, a Greek and a Latin library, and the Curia Octaviae. The south-eastern corner and the propylaeum survive. Two columns of the propylaeum's eastern front were removed and replaced by the large brick arch that still stands, painted with fresco, in the course of major works on the church at the end of the 1200s. From about 770 the church of San Paolo in summo circo, later Sant'Angelo in Pescheria, was built into the propylaeum. Augustus took part of the Circo Flaminio for the portico; the circus had been laid out by the censor Gaius Flaminius Nepos in 221 BC and nothing of it is visible today.

places.name: Teatro di Marcello
places.address: Via del Teatro di Marcello, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A Roman theatre carrying a Renaissance palace on top of it. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives it as visible from the outside only, open every day, 9.00 to 19.00 under summer time and 9.00 to 18.00 under winter time, entry free, closed on 1 May.
places.history: Julius Caesar began the theatre, expropriating the site and demolishing the temple of Pietas for it, and was criticised for doing so; Augustus took the work up. It was probably complete by 17 BC, when it was used for the ludi saeculares, and was dedicated in 13 or 11 BC in the name of Marcellus, the emperor's nephew, who had died at Baiae in 23 BC. Vespasian and Alexander Severus restored it. Its diameter is 130 metres and its capacity has been calculated at 15,000, or 20,000 at need; of the three orders of the travertine facade, two survive. The Pierleoni and the Fabi turned the ruin into a fortress. In the 1500s Baldassarre Peruzzi raised the Savelli palace on top of it, and the Orsini bought that in 1729. The Comune di Roma acquired the lower Roman part in the 1930s and excavated and restored it.

places.name: Tempio di Apollo Sosiano
places.summary: Three re-erected columns of a temple of Apollo, adjoining the Teatro di Marcello.
places.history: A cult of Apollo existed on the site by the middle of the 5th century BC. The first temple building was dedicated in 431 BC by the consul Gnaeus Julius after a plague, restored in 353 BC and worked on again in 179 BC. Gaius Sosius rebuilt it from about 34 BC, and the three standing columns belong to that rebuilding. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina describes a portico found in the late 1930s during the works to rebuild Santa Rita and the Palazzetto di Flaminio Ponzio, running along the east and north sides of the temple of Bellona toward the temple of Apollo, its piers part peperino and part brick faced with stucco imitating column fluting, with travertine paving.

places.name: Tempio di Bellona
places.summary: The podium of a Republican temple, adjoining the temple of Apollo Sosiano at the flank of the Teatro di Marcello.
places.history: Appius Claudius Caecus vowed the temple in 296 BC after a victory over the Etruscans. It stood outside the pomerium, and the Senate met in it when the business involved foreigners or serving commanders. The podium was found in the 1930s clearance around the Teatro di Marcello.

places.name: Foro Olitorio
places.summary: The site of the ancient vegetable market, between the Teatro di Marcello and the Foro Boario, on the street that still carries its name.
places.history: it.wikipedia describes a sacred area here with temples to Janus, Spes and Juno Sospita and a bronze elephant, the Elephas Herbarius. A fourth temple, built by Manius Acilius Glabrio, consul in 191 BC, stood next to the temple of Janus and was destroyed in the works for the Teatro di Marcello. Three of the temples are embedded in the basilica of San Nicola in Carcere, which was built over them.

places.name: Templi repubblicani di San Nicola in Carcere
places.summary: Three Republican temples embedded in the basilica of San Nicola in Carcere and its flanks. The identifications of the individual buildings are not certain: the Sovrintendenza Capitolina and it.wikipedia assign the dedications differently, and it.wikipedia states outright that the attribution of the individual buildings is not entirely settled.
places.history: The three temples were built between the first and second Punic wars, and a fourth was found by excavation nearby. The southern temple is Doric, possibly of Spes, and its columns are visible in the left wall of the church. The central temple measures 30 by 15 metres and is Ionic, probably of Juno Sospita, with remains visible in the crypt. The northern temple is Ionic, 26 by 15 metres, probably of Janus, with seven columns standing on one side and two on the other.

places.name: Monte Savello
places.address: Piazza di Monte Savello, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A low rise between the Tiber and the Capitol, and the square named after it. Palazzo Savelli Orsini stands on it, above the Teatro di Marcello.
places.history: it.wikipedia places Monte Savello in rione Sant'Angelo and explains the rise as the ruins of part of the Teatro di Marcello together with alluvium from the Tiber. It was known from at least the 12th century as monte Faffo or monte Fabiorum, and later took the name of the Savelli, whose palace was built on the theatre.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Angelo in Pescheria
places.address: Via della Tribuna di Campitelli 6, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The church built into the propylaeum of the Portico d'Ottavia, with three Corinthian columns of the portico set into its portal. It gives the rione its name. No source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The church was built in the 8th century inside the propylaeum. Pope Stephen II translated the relics of Symphorosa, Getulius and their seven sons here in 752, and the sarcophagus was found in 1610 with its inscription. In 1110 Paschal II made Saint Berard cardinal deacon of the title. From here, on Whit Sunday 1347, Cola di Rienzo set out to seize the Capitol. The chapel of Sant'Andrea was raised in 1571 as the seat of the fishmongers' company. Its altarpiece is by Giorgio Vasari; the vault fresco is not securely attributed. The organ is by Pietro Pantanella, 1877, with 25 stops, one manual and pedal, and wholly mechanical action. A Madonna and Child with angels in the church is attributed to Benozzo Gozzoli; it.wikipedia dates it 1447 to 1450 and Roma Capitale gives 1450.

places.name: Basilica di San Nicola in Carcere
places.summary: A basilica built over three Republican temples, whose columns show in its walls and crypt. it.wikipedia gives it as situated in rione Sant'Angelo, on via del Foro Olitorio. No source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: A first church stood here in the 6th century. A 10th-century inscription is cut on the column by the entrance, and the first reference to the church is a plaque of 1128 on the facade. The name comes from a prison on the site, the Byzantine Carcer ad Elephantum, which from the 13th century tradition confused with the Tullianum. The church was rebuilt in 1599, with a facade by Giacomo della Porta, keeping the medieval campanile, itself a converted Pierleoni tower. One of the bells is the one Pandolfo Savelli commissioned in 1289. The organ is by Nicola Morettini, 1908, with 9 stops. The basilica stands on its own because the medieval quarter around it was demolished in the mid-1920s.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli
places.summary: The church on piazza di Campitelli, in rione Sant'Angelo in spite of the name it carries. Its parish site gives Mass at 10.00 and 18.30 on feast days and 7.30 and 18.30 on weekdays.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the building belonged originally to rione Campitelli and was attributed to rione Sant'Angelo when Sant'Angelo's boundaries were extended around the middle of the twentieth century, after the clearances of the Fascist period. Clement VIII gave the older church to St John Leonardi and the Clerks Regular of the Mother of God on 4 August 1601. Rebuilding on the present site began on 29 September 1661, to Carlo Rainaldi, commissioned by Alexander VII to mark the end of the plague of 1656 and to house the Marian icon.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Caterina dei Funari
places.summary: A sixteenth-century church on the street of the rope-makers, in the block of the Isola Mattei. No source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The church is attested in a bull of Celestine III of 1192 as Sancta Maria dominae Rosae and as Sancta Maria in castro aureo, the second name from the ruins of the theatre of Balbus, which the Middle Ages called the castrum aureum. It is now named for the rope-makers of the quarter, who still give the street its name. In 1536 Paul III gave the church to Ignatius of Loyola, who founded a house for poor girls in the monastery. In 1560 Loyola suggested to Cardinal Federico Cesi, who paid for it, that the church be rebuilt and rededicated to Catherine of Alexandria; Guidetto Guidetti, a pupil of Michelangelo, took charge and the work was finished in 1564.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Ambrogio della Massima
places.summary: A church and a monastic complex on via di Sant'Ambrogio, with Roman rooms still visible in the basement.
places.history: The church is recorded in early catalogues of the city's churches as Sancta Maria de Maxima. By tradition it was built on the site of the house of Ambrose's father, and again by tradition the monastery was founded in 353 by Marcellina, elder sister of Ambrose and Satyrus. The convent stands on the area of the ancient Portico di Filippo, built by Lucius Marcius Philippus, Augustus's stepfather, in 29 BC around the temple of Hercules of the Muses, of which nothing survives. In 1876, after the Cessione dell'asse ecclesiastico, the monastic complex was divided between the Comune di Roma and the Cassinese Benedictines, who serve the church. The convent had extended over most of the block between via di Sant'Ambrogio, piazza Lovatelli and via di Sant'Angelo in Pescheria.

places.name: Chiesa di San Gregorio della Divina Pietà
places.summary: A small church facing ponte Fabricio, also called San Gregorio al Ponte Quattro Capi and San Gregorietto ai Quattro Capi. it.wikipedia gives it as in rione Sant'Angelo.
places.history: The first certain notice of the church is of 1403. It was restored in 1729 to designs by Filippo Barigioni for Benedict XIII and given to the Congregazione degli Operai della Divina Pietà, from which its name comes; the original alms box survives on the right side. It was restored again in 1858, when the bilingual inscription in Hebrew and Latin carrying a passage of scripture was set on the facade. The forced sermons imposed on the Jews of the ghetto under papal rule were preached here, and the double inscription records the practice.

places.name: Chiesa di Santo Stanislao dei Polacchi
places.address: Via delle Botteghe Oscure, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The national church of Poles in Rome, on via delle Botteghe Oscure. it.wikipedia gives it as in rione Sant'Angelo.
places.history: The church descends from San Salvatore in pensilis de Sorraca, a medieval church recorded in documents of 1174 and 1209 and built on the remains of the Circo Flaminio. An epigraph records a rebuilding of 27 October 1285 and is all that survives of the medieval church. Gregory XIII gave the church to the Polish cardinal Stanislaus Hosius, who had it wholly rebuilt in 1580 as the Polish national church.

places.name: Cappella di Santa Maria del Carmine e del Monte Libano
places.summary: A deconsecrated aedicule chapel on piazza Costaguti, on a half-oval plan with a half-dome carried on six columns and two half-columns. It is seen from the square; no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The chapel was built in 1759 by the devout of the neighbourhood and restored in 1825, which an inscription on the architrave records, again by the faithful in 1862, and again in 1876. It was profaned and then restored to worship in 1892. For much of the twentieth century a cobbler occupied it; it was then abandoned, and was recovered and conservatively restored in 2005 to a project by Arianna Cajano. Forced sermons to the Jews of the neighbouring ghetto were preached in the open square in front of it in the early evening.

places.name: Oratorio di Sant'Andrea dei pescivendoli
places.address: Via del Foro Piscario, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The deconsecrated oratory of the fishmongers' guild, adjoining Sant'Angelo in Pescheria. It is owned by the Comune di Roma and is now in commercial use, and is not open as a church.
places.history: The oratory was consecrated in 1689 as the oratory of the fishmongers' guild, and the words Locus orationis venditorum piscium still read above the portal. A high relief of Saint Andrew with a fish stands over the door, carved by Michel Maille with Lorenzo Ottoni.

places.name: Sala Santa Rita
places.summary: An exhibition space in a deconsecrated church, run by the Dipartimento Attività Culturali of Roma Capitale, which gives it as open when an exhibition is running.
places.history: Carlo Fontana built the church of Santa Rita da Cascia in Campitelli about 1650 to 1665 over the 11th-century San Biagio de Mercato, at the foot of the Aracoeli steps, designing the facade for a diagonal rather than a frontal view because of the narrow street it faced. The interior is octagonal with a small atrium. The church was dismantled stone by stone in 1928 and re-erected on the present site in 1937 to 1940, during the works that opened the via del Mare. The building returned to the Comune in 1990, was comprehensively restored around 2000 and reopened to the public with a new programme from April 2024.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria in Publicolis
places.summary: A seventeenth-century church on via in Publicolis. it.wikipedia gives it as situated in rione Sant'Angelo. The church is in the care of the Missionari dei Sacri Cuori di Gesù e Maria, who have their general house here.
places.history: The church was rebuilt in 1642 to 1643 by Giovanni Antonio De Rossi for Cardinal Marcello Santacroce.

places.name: Tempio Maggiore di Roma (Great Synagogue)
places.summary: The Great Synagogue of Rome, built between 1901 and 1904 and inaugurated in 1904, with a square-based dome clad in aluminium. It is visited on the Museo Ebraico's ticket, which includes a guided visit. The Tempio Spagnolo, an oratory for the Spanish rite, is in the same building.
places.history: The Fondazione Museo Ebraico's account is that after 1870 the Jewish communities of Europe were able to build monumental synagogues for the first time in centuries, and that Rome's was deliberately placed in the quarter the city's Jews had been shut into. In 1888 the Università ebraica contracted with the Comune for a site and the agreement was rescinded in 1896. A competition was held in 1889 calling for a building of carattere monumentale e severo, and Osvaldo Armanni and Vincenzo Costa won it. The synagogue went up on one of the four lots created when the decayed parts of the ghetto were demolished. The interior is richly decorated in art nouveau, and the bimah does not stand exactly in the Roman-rite position. The Tempio Spagnolo was placed in the building in 1932 and furnished in 1948 with the marble fittings of the Cinque Scole.

places.name: Museo Ebraico di Roma
places.summary: The museum of the Jewish community of Rome, inside the Tempio Maggiore complex, whose ticket includes a guided visit to the synagogue. Its 2026 hours run in bands: 1 to 26 October, Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 17.00, last admission 16.15, and Friday 9.00 to 14.00, last admission 13.15; 27 October to 9 November and 12 January to 8 February, Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 16.30, last admission 15.45, and Friday 9.00 to 14.00; 10 November to 11 January, Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 16.00, last admission 15.15, and Friday 9.00 to 14.00; 9 February to 31 March, Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 17.00 and Friday 9.00 to 14.00; and 1 April to 30 September, Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 18.00, last admission 17.15, and Friday 10.00 to 16.00, last admission 15.15. It is closed on Saturdays and on Jewish holidays and publishes a dated closure calendar. Admission is 12.00 euro full, 6.00 euro for students up to 25 with proof and 10.00 euro on the agreement rate, free for children under 10, for visitors with certified disability above 74 per cent and a companion where needed, for ICOM and ICOMOS card holders, for police and armed forces and for accredited journalists; online transactions carry a 1.00 euro service commission.
places.history: The museum opened in 1960 to hold the Roman community's collections, with a contribution from the Libyan Jewish community that arrived in 1967. It has seven rooms: Renaissance velvets and baroque embroidery, about 900 textiles of which some are in cases and some still in use in the city's synagogues; casts of inscriptions from the Roman catacombs and the synagogue of Ostia Antica, with medieval manuscripts and city plans; the Jewish year and the life cycle; and the treasures of the Cinque Scole, the silver, textiles and polychrome marble of the Scola del Tempio, the Scola Nova, the Scola Siciliana, the Scola Castigliana and the Scola Catalana. The museum also runs guided tours: the museum with the Tempio Maggiore and the Tempio Spagnolo at 100.00 euro for families and adult groups up to 25, plus admission, and walking tours of the Jewish quarter at 100.00 euro for one to four people, 150.00 euro for five to fifteen and 10.00 euro a head for sixteen to thirty-five, booked online at least five days ahead.

places.name: Fondazione Museo della Shoah, Casina dei Vallati
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 29, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The Fondazione Museo della Shoah ETS gives the Casina dei Vallati as its museum, at via del Portico d'Ottavia 29, open Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 18.00 and Friday 10.00 to 13.00 excluding Jewish holidays, closed Saturday. Its founding members are the Associazione figli della Shoah, the Comunità Ebraica di Roma, the Regione Lazio, Roma Capitale and the UCEI.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina's account of the building runs to its restoration of 1929 to 1932, to a project by Paolo Fidenzoni. The Casina was uncovered in the clearances begun in the 1920s to free the Teatro di Marcello, when substantial medieval fabric was found in the block being demolished and kept, after part of it had already collapsed. The corner toward the Portico d'Ottavia and via del Foro Piscario is Renaissance in character, with the original sixteenth-century marble portal and travertine window surrounds salvaged from another demolished palace and re-set here; the rest is thirteenth-century in character, with a first-floor loggia, a ground-floor portico and facing of tufelli and brick. The Sovrintendenza states that the building is named for the Vallati, who owned much property in this part of rione Sant'Angelo.

places.name: Antico quartiere ebraico (the Jewish quarter)
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: Roma Capitale describes the old Jewish quarter as situated inside Rione XI - Sant'Angelo. The Museo Ebraico defines the present quarter as four blocks, crossed lengthwise by via Catalana, which meets via del Tempio, bounded inside by via del Portico d'Ottavia and running to the Tiber.
places.history: The ghetto was instituted on 14 July 1555 by the bull Cum nimis absurdum of Paul IV, which revoked the community's rights and enclosed it behind a wall with two gates, opened at dawn and shut an hour after sunset between November and Easter and two hours after sunset in the rest of the year. The enclosure was trapezoidal, and the wall cut piazza Giudea in two. Christian owners of buildings inside kept them but, under the jus gazzagà, could neither evict their tenants nor raise the rents. About 2,000 Jews lived in Rome at the start of the 15th century, 1,200 of them in Sant'Angelo; in the plague of 1656, 800 of about 4,000 inhabitants of the quarter died. The gates were opened in 1798 under the Roman Republic and a tree of liberty was planted in piazza Giudea, and Napoleon's fall undid it. Pius IX ordered the wall demolished in 1847, and the work had to be done at night against Roman resistance. Only after 20 September 1870 did Roman Jews stop being second-class citizens. The quarter was demolished in 1885 and new building went up around the new synagogue. Brass plates set into the paving of the quarter, the pietre d'inciampo, each carry the name of a person deported and never returned.

places.name: Casa di Lorenzo Manilio
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 1, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A house of 1468 whose facade carries a long Latin inscription across a marble band, with its builder's name repeated on the architraves and ancient fragments set into the plaster of the base.
places.history: Roma Capitale's page for the rione carries the full Latin text with an Italian translation. It records that Lorenzo Manilio built the house from the foundations on piazza Giudea, for himself and his descendants, in the year 2221 from the foundation of Rome, at the age of 50 years, 3 months and 2 days, on the eleventh day before the calends of August. His name is repeated three times in Latin and once in Greek on the architraves, and the motto Ave Roma is cut on the windows.

places.name: Largo 16 Ottobre 1943
places.summary: A square in the Jewish quarter, named for the round-up carried out there in 1943 and carrying the community's commemorative plaque.
places.history: The square is named for 16 October 1943. Between 5.30 in the morning and two in the afternoon, SS and German order police, working from a census taken years earlier by the Fascist government, arrested 1,259 people here and in the surrounding streets, 689 women, 363 men and 207 children. Weeks earlier the community had been made to hand over fifty kilograms of gold against a promise of safety, and had done so. After foreign nationals and members of mixed families were released, 1,023 people were deported to Auschwitz; sixteen came back. The plaque in the square records 2,091 Roman Jews deported over the whole of the German occupation, of whom 101 returned. Of the 335 people killed at the Fosse Ardeatine on 24 March 1944, seventy-five belonged to the Roman Jewish community.

places.name: Largo Stefano Gaj Taché
places.address: Largo Stefano Gaj Taché, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The square at the Tempio Maggiore, named for a child killed in the attack on the synagogue in 1982.
places.history: The square carries the name of Stefano Gaj Taché, who was two years old. At 11.55 on Saturday 9 October 1982, Shemini Atzeret, and the day several dozen of the community's adolescents were celebrating their bar mitzvah, attackers threw grenades and fired on people leaving the Tempio Maggiore. He was killed by grenade fragments. About forty people were wounded, among them his parents and his four-year-old brother Gadiel.

places.name: Via del Portico d'Ottavia
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The spine of the Jewish quarter, running from the Portico d'Ottavia, with most of the rione's restaurants and food shops along it.
places.history: The fishmongers of the quarter sold on marble slabs rented at high prices from noble families. The copy of the marble slab that fixed the maximum length of fish that could be sold whole is on the wall by the Portico; Roma Capitale states that the original is in the Musei Capitolini, and carries the full inscription with a translation on its page for the rione.

places.name: Via della Reginella
places.summary: A narrow street of old ghetto fabric running off piazza Mattei, with Palazzo Costaguti on one corner and a handful of small shops and galleries along it.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that via della Reginella was taken into the enclosure of the ghetto only at the beginning of the nineteenth century, and that the quarter around it was demolished in 1885.

places.name: Isola Mattei
places.summary: A whole block of Mattei family palaces, between via delle Botteghe Oscure, via Michelangelo Caetani, via dei Funari, piazza Mattei, via Paganica and piazza dell'Enciclopedia Italiana. it.wikipedia gives it as situated in rione Sant'Angelo.
places.history: The Mattei built the Isola between the 15th and 17th centuries on the remains of the theatre of Balbus. In the Middle Ages the site was the Castrum Aureum, nominally the property of the convent of Santa Maria Dominae Rosae, now Santa Caterina dei Funari. From the 13th century it held the houses of the Crescenzi, the Piermattei degli Albertoni, the Saragona, the Coccia, the Mellini, the de Ambrosinis and the Malabranca, and at the end of the 14th century it was broken up and sold.

places.name: Palazzo Mattei di Giove
places.summary: The Mattei palace that stands between via Michelangelo Caetani and via dei Funari, in the block of the Isola Mattei, and is also known as Antici Mattei and Mattei ai Funari.
places.history: The palace was built for Asdrubale Mattei, duke of Giove, and begun in 1598 to a design by Carlo Maderno; the linking wing was begun in 1613 and finished in 1618. The male Mattei di Giove line died out at the start of the 19th century and the palace passed to Marianna Mattei, wife of Carlo Teodoro Antici. it.wikipedia records four institutions in the building: the Biblioteca di storia moderna e contemporanea and the Istituto Centrale per i Beni Sonori e Audiovisivi, both of the Ministero della cultura, the Centro Studi Americani, and the Istituto storico italiano per l'età moderna e contemporanea.

places.name: Palazzo Caetani
places.address: Via delle Botteghe Oscure 32, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The palace houses the embassy of Brazil to the Holy See, the Fondazione Camillo Caetani, offices of the Fondazione Roffredo Caetani and the FAI Rome delegation.
places.history: It was built for Alessandro Mattei between 1545 and 1564, and acquired by the Caetani in 1776, from whom the present name comes; it is also called Mattei Caetani and Mattei alle Botteghe Oscure. The architect is not settled: Ammannati has often been given and has recently been doubted, and Baglione mentions a contribution by Vignola without saying whether he designed it. it.wikipedia's article on the street records the Fondazione Camillo Caetani in the building since 1963.

places.name: Palazzo Mattei di Paganica
places.summary: Palazzo Mattei di Paganica, on piazza dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, is the seat of the Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana, founded in Rome on 18 February 1925 by Giovanni Treccani and Giovanni Gentile.
places.history: The palace is one of the Mattei buildings of the Isola Mattei, on the square that was formerly piazza Paganica and took its present name from the Institute. The Institute was founded as the Istituto Giovanni Treccani.

places.name: Palazzo di Giacomo Mattei
places.summary: One of the two earlier Mattei palaces facing piazza Mattei, named by it.wikipedia among the Roman buildings that carry the Mattei name.
places.history: Roma Capitale's page for piazza Mattei describes the low unadorned facades of the two older Mattei palaces on the square, one built at the end of the fifteenth century and the other in the first half of the sixteenth, probably by Nanni di Baccio Bigio for the sons of Mattei.

places.name: Palazzo Costaguti
places.summary: A sixteenth-century palace on the corner of piazza Mattei and via della Reginella, running along via dei Falegnami with rear facades on piazza Costaguti. It is the seat of Universitas Mercatorum, a telematic university. No source states that its frescoed interiors can be visited.
places.history: The palace was built in the first half of the sixteenth century for Monsignor Costanzo Patrizi, treasurer to Paul III, on the site of the demolished church of San Leonardo de Albis. On Patrizi's death in 1578 it was sold to Ascanio and Prospero Costaguti, Genoese bankers, for 26,000 scudi, and Carlo Lambardi renovated it for them between 1597 and 1619. Roma Capitale records ceilings frescoed by Guercino, Domenichino and Lanfranco among others.

places.name: Palazzo Guglielmi Chiablese
places.summary: A palace at the corner of piazza dell'Enciclopedia Italiana with via Paganica, holding the Biblioteca dell'Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana.
places.history: The palace was built in 1776 for Benedetto di Savoia, duke of Chiablese. It was sold to the Guglielmi, who rebuilt it entirely around 1880 into its present form; the wing facing the square was added after the old church of Santi Sebastiano e Valentino dei Mercanti, which stood in the middle of the square, was demolished. The library was founded with the Institute in 1925, and in 1926 Giovanni Gentile endowed it with the private collection of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century encyclopaedias and lexicons of the engineer Aldo Santi, the puzzle-setter known as Duca Borso.

places.name: Palazzo Savelli Orsini
places.summary: The palace built on top of the Teatro di Marcello at Monte Savello. It houses the embassy of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta to the Holy See.
places.history: Baldassarre Peruzzi raised the palace in the 1500s for the Savelli on the ruins of the theatre, which was already a medieval fortress of the Pierleoni and the Fabi. In 1729 Ferdinando Bernualdo Filippo Orsini d'Aragona, of the dukes of Gravina, bought it for 29,000 scudi; Benedict XIII, of the same family, had legitimated him to the Roman Orsini succession. The new owners moved the family archive there from the palazzo di Monte Giordano and added three ranges around the garden, entered from the square through a gate between piers carrying the family's heraldic bears. The painter Giacomo Zoboli lived there from 1760 until his death in 1767.

places.name: Palazzo Caetani Lovatelli
places.summary: The palace on piazza Lovatelli, named in it.wikipedia's article on the rione as Palazzo Caetani Lovatelli, su piazza Lovatelli. It was formerly the Serlupi palace.
places.history: it.wikipedia's article on piazza di Campitelli records that the medieval church of Santa Maria in Campitello stood where the palace now is. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that piazza Lovatelli was formerly piazza Serlupi, from the family that built its residence there in 1580.

places.name: Sovrintendenza Capitolina ai Beni Culturali (piazza Lovatelli)
places.summary: The working seat of the Sovrintendenza Capitolina ai Beni Culturali, the arm of Roma Capitale that looks after the city's own monuments and museums. It gives its own address as piazza Lovatelli 35.
places.history: The seat is two buildings, of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, that replaced and partly absorbed medieval units on the square. The facade was restructured in 1764 on a survey by Luigi Vanvitelli, who gave it the flat rustication; on the via di Sant'Angelo in Pescheria flank the original look survives, with false rustication incised in the plaster. Two rooms retain frescoes and stucco, and the altana and the main portal on the square survive. The buildings were restored in the 1990s to a project by a team led by Paolo Marconi. They were historically tied to the convent of Sant'Ambrogio della Massima, which from the seventeenth century owned both.

places.name: Palazzo Clementi
places.summary: A palace on piazza di Campitelli, standing where a medieval tower was absorbed into a Renaissance house.
places.history: it.wikipedia's article on piazza di Campitelli records that the palace stands where the tower called del Merangolo, or Citrangolo, was absorbed into the house of Fabrizio de Massimi.

places.name: Palazzetto di Flaminio Ponzio
places.summary: A 1950s block closing the short east end of piazza di Campitelli, carrying a facade that was built somewhere else. It is an office of the Comune's Dipartimento IV.
places.history: Flaminio Ponzio, born 1559 or 1560 and died in Rome in 1613, built the original in 1600 on via Alessandrina, in rione Monti, and it was demolished in 1933 for the opening of via dei Fori Imperiali. The architectural elements of the front were dismantled and kept, and re-erected here twenty-odd years later. The mascaron of the central window was re-carved during the 1950s work, on the model of the original.

places.name: Albergo della Catena
places.address: Via della Tribuna di Campitelli, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A medieval inn set against the temple of Apollo Sosiano, three merged units on an L plan. It was in the past the institutional seat of the Sovrintendenza Capitolina.
places.history: The building went up between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries as an inn. It is named for a chain that barred the alley then called della Catena di Pescheria; the Sovrintendenza Capitolina explains the practice, in which chains marked out a property, or kept carts away from hospitals and hospices, or, at a noble palace, showed when taut that the owner was away. The Comune bought the building in 1929 for the widening of the via del Mare and it was slated for demolition. It was not demolished but restructured in 1929 to 1930, isolating the medieval part, and the alley itself disappeared in 1933.

places.name: Torre dei Grassi
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A medieval tower set against the Portico d'Ottavia, between via di Sant'Angelo in Pescheria, via della Tribuna di Campitelli and via del Portico d'Ottavia. it.wikipedia gives it as in rione Sant'Angelo.
places.history: The tower was built in phases from perhaps the twelfth century. It was called Fornicata for its shape and dei Grassi for the family who bought it from the Orsini in 1369. The Ospedale di Santa Maria della Consolazione bought it in 1481.

places.name: Villino Lupi
places.address: Piazza delle Cinque Scole 37, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: An early twentieth-century villino at the corner of via Catalana. it.wikipedia gives it as in rione Sant'Angelo and names it among the rione's architecture.
places.history: The building belongs to the clearance of the ghetto begun in 1885, which was slowed by the building crisis of 1888 and the failure of the Banca Tiberina. The plot was divided in 1909 and the villino was finished in 1910 to a design by Romolo Gui. In 1925 Salvatore Rebecchini submitted a scheme to add a storey and a Guelph crenellation to the attic.

places.name: Fontana delle Tartarughe
places.summary: The fountain in piazza Mattei: four bronze ephebes playing with dolphins on shell basins, with four turtles on the rim of the upper basin. The turtles in place now are copies.
places.history: The fountain was made between 1581 and 1588 to a design by Giacomo della Porta, 1533 to 1602, with sculpture by the Florentine Taddeo Landini, 1550 to 1596. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the materials as africano, pavonazzetto, white and bigio marble, travertine and bronze, and the original supply as the Acqua Vergine. A fountain had been decided for piazza Giudea in 1570, and the nobleman Muzio Mattei prevailed on the administration to move it to the square his own house faced, undertaking in exchange to have the square paved at his expense and to keep the fountain clean. Four of the eight intended dolphins were never installed because the water pressure would not lift them, and went to the Fontana della Terrina. The four turtles, traditionally attributed to Bernini, were added in the restoration of 1658 to 1659 under Alexander VII, which four marble cartouches record. Roma Capitale records that the turtles were stolen in 1906, in 1944 and in 1981, and that three surviving originals are in the Musei Capitolini. The fountain was restored in 2005 to 2006 with new water treatment, and again in 2025 under the PNRR Caput Mundi programme.

places.name: Edicola sacra della Madonna Annunciata, palazzetto dell'Olmo
places.address: Via delle Botteghe Oscure 34, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A street shrine on a fifteenth-century building that belonged to the Mattei: a painting under glass in a gilt stucco frame with a tympanum and the dove of the Holy Spirit, lilies and a cartouche reading Mater Providine. It is known both as the Madonna della Provvidenza and as the Madonna dell'Annunciata.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that written and oral testimony puts the shrine originally between piazza Mattei and piazza Paganica, in what was historically the contrada dell'Olmo. During restoration in the 1970s the signature of Vincenzo Milone was found, dating the work to 1788, and a record of a further restoration in 1898 came to light in the same work. Three marble epigraphs below the shrine refer to the movement of the Virgin's eyes in the summer of 1796, during the French invasion; the Sovrintendenza states that about twenty-five images in Rome were officially recognised by cardinalatial decree as subject to such events.

places.name: Museo Nazionale Romano - Crypta Balbi
places.address: Via delle Botteghe Oscure 31, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: Roma Capitale states that from 9 January 2023 the Crypta Balbi has been closed to the public for the works connected with the URBS project, dalla città alla campagna romana. No reopening date is stated. It is one of the four seats of the Museo Nazionale Romano, with Palazzo Massimo, Palazzo Altemps and the Terme di Diocleziano.
places.history: The site is the porticoed courtyard behind the theatre that Lucius Cornelius Balbus built and dedicated in 13 BC, together with everything that built up over it: the Roman crypta and the south side of the Porticus Minucia, the early-medieval church and convent of Santa Maria Domine Rose, the medieval houses of via dei Delfini, a Renaissance convent of Santa Caterina with its conservatorio, and an eighteenth-century Polish hospice. About 7,000 square metres was acquired by the State in 1981. Roma Capitale describes a display on three levels: the archaeology of the Balbus complex and the neighbouring Porticus on the ground floor, the buildings raised against the Crypta after the fire of 80 AD and abandoned in the seventh century on the first, and the changes from late antiquity to the Middle Ages on the second. The museum rooms are in the seventeenth-century dormitory of the convent of Santa Caterina. The theatre itself was built in stone with the spoils of Balbus's victory over the Garamantes and dedicated in 13 BC; it burnt under Titus, probably in 79, and was restored, probably by Domitian. It measured 95 metres in diameter and held 7,700 spectators. Medieval shops in its arcades gave via delle Botteghe Oscure its name, and the rope-makers who gave via dei Funari its name twisted their rope in the 60-metre porticoed courtyard.

places.name: Piazza Mattei
places.summary: The square the Fontana delle Tartarughe stands in, at the edge of the Isola Mattei, with Palazzo Costaguti on one corner and two earlier Mattei palaces facing it.
places.history: Roma Capitale's page for the square describes the low unadorned facades of the two older Mattei palaces on it, one built at the end of the fifteenth century and the other in the first half of the sixteenth, probably by Nanni di Baccio Bigio for the sons of Mattei. The fountain came to the square in the 1580s after Muzio Mattei persuaded the administration to move it from piazza Giudea.

places.name: Piazza Lovatelli
places.summary: A small square holding Palazzo Caetani Lovatelli and, at no. 35, the seat of the Sovrintendenza Capitolina ai Beni Culturali.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the square was formerly piazza Serlupi, from the family that built its residence there in 1580. The convent of Sant'Ambrogio della Massima, which from the seventeenth century owned the buildings that are now the Sovrintendenza's seat, extended over most of the block between the square, via di Sant'Ambrogio and via di Sant'Angelo in Pescheria.

places.name: Piazza Costaguti
places.summary: The square behind Palazzo Costaguti, which shows its rear facades on it. The deconsecrated Cappella di Santa Maria del Carmine e del Monte Libano stands on the square, and the Antico Forno Urbani is at no. 31.
places.history: The square takes its name from the Costaguti, the Genoese bankers who bought the palace on it from the heirs of Monsignor Costanzo Patrizi in 1578. Forced sermons to the Jews of the neighbouring ghetto were preached in the open square in front of the chapel in the early evening.

places.name: Piazza dell'Enciclopedia Italiana (formerly piazza Paganica)
places.summary: The square at the north-east corner of the Isola Mattei, carrying Palazzo Mattei di Paganica and Palazzo Guglielmi Chiablese. it.wikipedia lists it under both its present name and its former one, piazza Paganica; via Paganica and vicolo Paganica are separate streets.
places.history: The old church of Santi Sebastiano e Valentino dei Mercanti stood in the middle of the square and was demolished; the wing of Palazzo Guglielmi Chiablese that faces the square was added afterwards. The square takes its present name from the Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana, whose seat is Palazzo Mattei di Paganica.

places.name: Piazza di Campitelli
places.summary: A square in rione Sant'Angelo that carries a neighbouring rione's name. Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli stands at no. 9, the Palazzetto di Flaminio Ponzio closes the short east end at no. 6, and Palazzo Clementi stands on it.
places.history: it.wikipedia's article on the square says that it takes its name from the rione of the same name. It records that the medieval church of Santa Maria in Campitello stood where Palazzo Caetani Lovatelli now is, and that Palazzo Clementi stands where the tower called del Merangolo was absorbed into the house of Fabrizio de Massimi. The church on the square was attributed to rione Sant'Angelo when Sant'Angelo's boundaries were extended around the middle of the twentieth century.

places.name: Centro di Documentazione dell'Appia
places.address: Via del Teatro di Marcello 5, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A documentation centre for the via Appia, run by the Sovrintendenza Capitolina, which lists it among its own places at via del Teatro di Marcello 5. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The centre is one of the facilities of the Sovrintendenza Capitolina ai Beni Culturali, whose seat is at piazza Lovatelli 35 in the same rione.

places.name: Pasticceria Boccione
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 1, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A bakery on via del Portico d'Ottavia. Roma Capitale's page for the rione names it for its torta di visciole e ricotta, a sour cherry and ricotta tart. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale names the shop on its page for rione Sant'Angelo, among the things to eat in the quarter.

places.name: Antico Forno Urbani
places.summary: A bakery on piazza Costaguti. Roma Capitale's page for the rione names it for its pizza by the slice. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale names the forno on its page for rione Sant'Angelo, among the things to eat in the quarter.

places.name: Trattoria Giggetto al Portico d'Ottavia
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 21/A, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A Roman trattoria on via del Portico d'Ottavia, in Roma Capitale's register of historic shops of excellence. Roma Capitale gives the hours as Tuesday to Sunday, 12.30 to 15.00 and 19.30 to 23.00, closed Monday, and gives the site as giggettoalportico.it.
places.history: Roma Capitale's account is that Luigi Ceccarelli, called Giggetto, founded the osteria with his wife Ines in 1923; that their son Franco and his wife Lidia carried it on; and that it is now with Claudio and Marco Ceccarelli, in the third generation.

places.name: Nonna Betta
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 16, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A Roman Jewish restaurant on via del Portico d'Ottavia. Its own site gives 12.15 to 15.00 and 18.30 to 22.00, closed Tuesday.
places.history: The restaurant stands on the street that runs from the Portico d'Ottavia through the old Jewish quarter.

places.name: BellaCarne
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 51, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A kosher restaurant on via del Portico d'Ottavia. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The restaurant is one of the kosher kitchens along the street through the old Jewish quarter.

places.name: La Taverna del Ghetto
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 8, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant on via del Portico d'Ottavia that also runs a cooking class. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The restaurant is one of the kitchens along the street through the old Jewish quarter.

places.name: Ba'Ghetto
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 57, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A kosher restaurant on via del Portico d'Ottavia. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: It is the meat kitchen of a pair on the same street; the dairy kitchen, Ba'Ghetto Milky, is at no. 2.

places.name: Ba'Ghetto Milky
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 2, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The dairy kitchen of Ba'Ghetto, on via del Portico d'Ottavia. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The meat kitchen of the same house is at no. 57 on the same street.

places.name: Renato al Ghetto
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 5, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant on via del Portico d'Ottavia. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The restaurant is one of the kitchens along the street through the old Jewish quarter.

places.name: La Reginella d'Italia
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 65, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant on via del Portico d'Ottavia. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The restaurant takes its name from via della Reginella, the narrow street of old ghetto fabric that runs off piazza Mattei.

places.name: La Dolceroma
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 20, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: An Austrian pastry shop on via del Portico d'Ottavia. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale's page for the Jewish quarter mentions an Austrian pastry shop among the bakeries of the quarter.

places.name: Kosher Delight
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 11, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A kosher food shop on via del Portico d'Ottavia. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The shop is one of the kosher businesses along the street through the old Jewish quarter.

places.name: Le Tartarughe
places.summary: A cafe on piazza Mattei, named for the fountain in the square. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The cafe stands on the square where the Fontana delle Tartarughe was set up in the 1580s.

places.name: Grezzo Raw Chocolate
places.summary: A raw chocolate and ice cream shop on piazza Mattei. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The shop stands on the square with the Fontana delle Tartarughe.

places.name: Gelateria Steccolecco
places.address: Via del Portico d'Ottavia 6, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: An ice cream shop on via del Portico d'Ottavia. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The shop stands on the street that runs through the old Jewish quarter.

places.name: Peperita
places.summary: A chilli shop on via della Reginella. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The shop stands on the narrow street of old ghetto fabric that runs off piazza Mattei.

places.name: ALEFBET, the Hebrew letters art gallery
places.summary: A gallery of work built on the Hebrew letters, on via della Reginella. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The gallery stands on the narrow street of old ghetto fabric that runs off piazza Mattei.

places.name: F.A.D. room
places.summary: A small gallery on via della Reginella. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The gallery stands on the narrow street of old ghetto fabric that runs off piazza Mattei.

places.name: Ristorante Il Fantino
places.address: Via di Sant'Angelo in Pescheria 14, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant on via di Sant'Angelo in Pescheria. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The restaurant stands on the street named for the church built into the propylaeum of the Portico d'Ottavia.

places.name: AquaMadre Hammam
places.summary: A hammam on via di Sant'Ambrogio. Its own site describes a sequence of rooms on the Roman model: an apodyterium, a tepidarium at 34 degrees and a calidarium at 45 degrees and 100 per cent humidity.
places.history: The baths stand on the street of the church and convent of Sant'Ambrogio della Massima.

places.name: Hosianum Palace
places.summary: A hotel on via dei Polacchi. Its own site describes a historic residence in a sixteenth-century building, with 28 rooms.
places.history: The hotel takes its name from Cardinal Stanislaus Hosius, the Polish cardinal who had Santo Stanislao dei Polacchi wholly rebuilt in 1580 as the Polish national church. The street is named for the same community.

entries.name: Portico d'Ottavia
entries.note: Augustus rebuilt it between 27 and 23 BC and dedicated it in his sister's name; Septimius Severus and Caracalla rebuilt most of what stands, in 203.

entries.name: Teatro di Marcello
entries.note: Begun by Julius Caesar and dedicated in 13 or 11 BC in the name of Augustus's nephew; the Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives it as free, open daily, and seen from the outside only.

entries.name: Tempio Maggiore di Roma
entries.note: The Great Synagogue, built between 1901 and 1904 to Osvaldo Armanni and Vincenzo Costa's winning design, with a square-based dome clad in aluminium.

entries.name: Museo Ebraico di Roma
entries.note: Seven rooms of textiles, inscriptions and the treasures of the Cinque Scole; the ticket includes a guided visit to the synagogue, and the museum is closed on Saturdays.

entries.name: Fondazione Museo della Shoah, Casina dei Vallati
entries.note: The Fondazione gives its museum at via del Portico d'Ottavia 29, open Sunday to Thursday 10.00 to 18.00 and Friday 10.00 to 13.00, closed Saturday.

entries.name: Antico quartiere ebraico
entries.note: The quarter enclosed by the bull Cum nimis absurdum on 14 July 1555, its wall pulled down on Pius IX's order in 1847 and the quarter itself demolished in 1885.

entries.name: Largo 16 Ottobre 1943
entries.note: The square where 1,259 people were arrested on 16 October 1943; the plaque records 2,091 Roman Jews deported over the whole occupation, of whom 101 returned.

entries.name: Fontana delle Tartarughe
entries.note: Della Porta's design of 1581 to 1588 with Taddeo Landini's bronzes; the turtles were added in 1658 to 1659 and the ones in place now are copies.

entries.name: Chiesa di Sant'Angelo in Pescheria
entries.note: The church built into the propylaeum of the Portico d'Ottavia, from which Cola di Rienzo set out on Whit Sunday 1347 to seize the Capitol.

entries.name: Basilica di San Nicola in Carcere
entries.note: Three Republican temples are embedded in its walls and crypt; the campanile is a converted Pierleoni tower and one bell was commissioned by Pandolfo Savelli in 1289.

entries.name: Isola Mattei
entries.note: A whole block the Mattei built between the 15th and 17th centuries over the remains of the theatre of Balbus, holding four of their palaces.

entries.name: Museo Nazionale Romano - Crypta Balbi
entries.note: Roma Capitale states it has been closed to the public since 9 January 2023 for works connected with the URBS project, with no reopening date given.

entries.name: Trattoria Giggetto al Portico d'Ottavia
entries.note: Roma Capitale records Luigi Ceccarelli founding the osteria with his wife Ines in 1923, and gives the hours as Tuesday to Sunday, closed Monday.

entries.name: Pasticceria Boccione
entries.note: The bakery Roma Capitale names on its page for the rione, for its torta di visciole e ricotta, a sour cherry and ricotta tart.

The neighbour across via delle Botteghe Oscure and via Florida. The Area Sacra di Largo Argentina and its four temples are there, not here.
The neighbour across piazza delle Cinque Scole and via di Santa Maria del Pianto, holding Palazzo Cenci and several restaurants people call the Ghetto's.
